title: VPS or shared hosting: which one pays off for your site on Hostinger
seoTitle: VPS or shared hosting: which to choose
description: An ordinary site does fine on shared hosting; a VPS only with your own system, reserved resources or root access. Chart by scenario and KVM specs.
metaDescription: VPS or shared hosting at Hostinger: what each one is, a chart by scenario, the specs of KVM 1 to 8 and what maintenance is left to you.
imageAlt: Hostinger logo with the icons of an ordinary website and of a server, one against the other

contentSections.heading: Quick answer
paragraphs: For an ordinary site, a blog, a portfolio or a small shop, shared hosting does the job and costs less. A VPS only pays off when the site needs a system installed outside the control panel, reserved CPU and memory, or root access. See the verdict below.

contentSections.heading: What each one is
paragraphs: **Shared hosting** is one server split between several customers. Hostinger looks after the operating system, the web server and the updates; you log in to the control panel, install WordPress or upload your site's files, and that is it. At Hostinger, these are the Single, Premium and Unlimited plans, plus Cloud Startup, which is the same idea with more resources.

A **VPS** (virtual private server) is a virtual machine of your own, with reserved processor, memory and disk. Hostinger hands you the machine with the operating system and root access, the user that can do anything. From there on, installing the web server, the database and the certificate, plus updates and security, are your jobs. At Hostinger, these are the KVM 1, 2, 4 and 8 plans.
The difference is not “better or worse”. It is who looks after the server and how much of its resources are reserved for you.

contentSections.heading: Which to choose, by scenario
paragraphs: Before you look at prices, answer three questions. If the answer is “no” to all three, shared hosting will do.

contentSections.heading: The VPS plans: KVM 1 to 8
paragraphs: The four KVM plans differ only in size. Specs read on Hostinger's VPS page on October 28, 2026.
postParagraphs: For an ordinary site that needs a VPS, KVM 1 is the starting point: 4 GB of RAM is enough for a WordPress site or a small system. KVM 2 comes in when you will run more than one program on the same machine. KVM 4 and 8 are for a larger system, a big database or several applications.

contentSections.heading: Maintenance: what is left to you
paragraphs: This is the part the price does not show. On shared hosting, Hostinger maintains the server and the panel; you look after your site (theme, plugins, content). The Premium plan lists weekly backups, and Unlimited includes priority support.
On a VPS, Hostinger says on its own page that, with root access, the server's configuration, updates and security are up to whoever signed up. In practice, it becomes a list of yours:
bullets: **Install and configure** the web server, the database and the SSL certificate.
**Update** the operating system and the programs, from time to time.
**Secure it**: firewall, open ports, passwords and access keys.
**Back up** and know how to restore.
**Fix it** when the site goes down outside business hours.
postParagraphs: If you have never opened a terminal, this has a cost: either learning time or someone to do it for you. For an ordinary site, that cost is usually bigger than the price difference between the plans.

contentSections.heading: When a VPS makes sense for an AI agent
paragraphs: One case where a VPS often comes in is not a website: it is an AI assistant running all day, like OpenClaw. Then the question changes, because Hostinger also sells a managed plan for these assistants. If that is your case, the comparison is in [OpenClaw at Hostinger: managed or VPS](/en/reviews/openclaw-hostinger-managed-or-vps) and, to pick the size, in [which KVM for OpenClaw](/en/reviews/best-vps-for-openclaw). This article stays on the website server.

contentSections.heading: Verdict: VPS or shared hosting
contentSections.emphasis: If it were for my own site, I would take Premium, because it costs less and Hostinger looks after the server.
paragraphs: **Shared hosting** for a blog, portfolio, company site, small shop and Node.js site. Server maintenance is Hostinger's job. Among the plans, Premium is the starting point; if the site grows, Unlimited or Cloud Startup, before you think of a VPS.

**VPS** for your own system, a program or database outside the panel, a bot or dashboard running all day, or when you need root. Start with KVM 1 and move up if memory runs short. Count in the time it takes to maintain the server, or the cost of someone who does it.
**When in doubt, shared hosting.** A VPS does not turn into shared hosting later, but going the other way is just a new contract when the need appears.

contentSections.heading: Frequently asked questions
bullets: Is a VPS faster than shared hosting? We did not measure it. What a VPS guarantees is reserved resources: CPU, memory and disk are yours, while on shared hosting the server is divided. For an ordinary site, that is rarely the bottleneck.

Can I start on shared hosting and move to a VPS later? Yes. They are different products: you sign up for the VPS, install the server and move the site over. Shared hosting cannot be converted into a VPS from inside the panel.

Do I need to know Linux to have a VPS? Yes, the basics of the terminal: installing programs, updating the system and reading a log. On shared hosting, everything goes through the panel and no terminal is required.
Can a VPS run WordPress? It can, but you install and maintain the web server, PHP and the database. On shared hosting, WordPress comes ready in the panel and Hostinger looks after the server.
